::: {#case .lx-sec}
```{=html}
<div class="lx-case">
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">1 · The puzzle</p><p>A factory usually goes where land is cheap and its customers are close. If it can make its own power and sell what it does not use, does a windy, sunny site far away start to look better?</p></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">2 · The question in one sentence</p><p class="lx-case-q">Where should a manufacturing supply chain place its facilities, and how much on-site wind, solar and storage should each facility install when facilities can trade energy with the grid?</p><p class="lx-hint">Question type: prescriptive (where should it build, and what should each site install?).</p></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">3 · Scale and boundary</p><ul><li><b>Inside:</b> a stylized supply chain of factories, warehouses and retail stores, with candidate sites in California, Arizona and Nevada, over one year: production week by week, energy hour by hour (52 weeks of 168 hours).</li><li><b>Left out:</b> real distances and costs, which are synthetic; grid outages; the rest of the grid, which enters through hourly buying and selling prices.</li></ul></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">4 · Decisions, goal and rules, in words</p><ul><li><b>Decisions:</b> which candidate factories and warehouses to open, how products move through the network, how much wind, solar and storage each open site installs, and what it buys and sells every hour.</li><li><b>Goal:</b> the lowest net cost of the supply chain (facilities, production, inventory, transport and energy), less what energy sales earn.</li><li><b>Rules:</b> each open site balances its energy every hour; weekly store demand is met at a set service level (a <span class="lx-term" data-term="chance-constraint">chance constraint</span>).</li></ul></div>
<div class="lx-case-part wide"><p class="lx-eyebrow">5 · Data and method</p><ul><li>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="mixed-integer-program">mixed-integer model</span> opens factories and warehouses, routes products and sizes each open site's wind, solar and storage, with an hourly energy balance and grid trade.</li><li>Uncertain weekly store demand enters as a chance constraint with a set service level, written as its <span class="lx-term" data-term="deterministic-equivalent">deterministic equivalent</span>, so the model stays a mixed-integer linear program.</li></ul></div>
<div class="lx-case-part wide"><p class="lx-eyebrow">6 · What came out, and where it holds</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:supply-chain-mg"><p>When each facility can install its own wind, solar and storage and trade energy with the grid, a candidate site's renewable resource affects its operating cost.</p><p>Because the <span class="lx-term" data-term="transactive-energy">transactive energy</span> market brought a new revenue stream, locations with stronger renewables became competitive to establish facilities despite higher fixed and <span class="lx-term" data-term="logistics-cost">logistics cost</span>.</p><p>Transactive energy, <span class="lx-term" data-term="time-of-use">time-of-use</span> tariffs and climate conditions played a critical role in locating factories, warehouses, wind turbines, solar photovoltaics and energy storage systems.</p><p>Contrary to intuition, energy storage systems, which balance intermittent power and uncertain load, had limited benefits for cost saving.</p><footer>From: Li et al. (2023), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apm.2023.02.014">Applied Mathematical Modelling</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<ul class="lx-hint cf1-holds"><li>Holds when: <span class="lx-term" data-term="stylized-network">stylized networks</span> with synthetic distances and costs, candidate sites in California, Arizona and Nevada, and one year, planned week by week for products and hour by hour for energy.</li><li>Leaves out: grid outages, which the studies do not model.</li></ul></div>
</div>
<div class="lx-interactive" data-learn="cf1" data-src="../assets/learn/data/cf1-supply-chain-microgrids.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The studies in time</p>
<!-- cf1-timeline:start (written from the data file by LX.Timeline's staticHTML in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->

Factories, warehouses and their on-site microgrids are sited and sized together, for a three-tier supply chain over one year; published online in February 2023, in the July 2023 issue. <span class="lx-hint">Source: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apm.2023.02.014">Li et al. (2023), Applied Mathematical Modelling 119, 119–136</a></span></li><li><b>June 2023</b> · Conference paper. A two-tier version locates warehouses and sizes their microgrids, with electric-truck routing and electricity trading. <span class="lx-hint">Source: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/SEGRE58867.2023.00071">Li et al. (2023), SEGRE 2023, 410–415</a></span></li><li><b>30 October 2026</b> · Code released. A documented, runnable implementation of the location models, with synthetic examples (version 1.0.1). <span class="lx-hint">Source: <a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/supply-chain-microgrid-models">supply-chain-microgrid-models on GitHub</a>, as of 3 November 2026</span></li></ol>

## The idea behind it, then where the result holds
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-interactive" data-learn="cf1-idea" data-src="../assets/learn/data/cf1-supply-chain-microgrids.json ../assets/learn/data/town_year.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- cf1-idea:start (written from the toy model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">One factory, two sites (illustrative)</p><table class="lx-facts cf1-assume"><caption class="lx-hint">The toy's two sites (illustrative, 2025 dollars)</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col"></th><th scope="col">Near site</th><th scope="col">Windy site</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Site and building, a year</th><td class="n">$1.00M</td><td class="n">$1.15M</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Shipping to the stores, a year</th><td class="n">$0.60M</td><td class="n">$1.00M</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Wind <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-factor">capacity factor</span></th><td class="n">25%</td><td class="n">42%</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Solar capacity factor</th><td class="n">18%</td><td class="n">26%</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="lx-hint">Both: a flat 3 <span class="lx-term" data-term="megawatt">MW</span> factory load; grid power bought at $80/<span class="lx-term" data-term="megawatt-hour">MWh</span>; wind $170,000 and solar $85,000 per MW a year; room for up to 8 MW of each.</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table cf1-res"><caption class="lx-hint">Which site wins, and what each builds (the toy, a year)</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Setting</th><th scope="col">Cheaper site</th><th scope="col">Near site builds</th><th scope="col">Windy site builds</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">No on-site energy</th><td>Near site, by $550k a year</td><td>–</td><td>–</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Spare energy sold for nothing</th><td>Near site, by $83k a year</td><td>0 MW wind · 5 MW solar</td><td>5 MW wind · 2 MW solar</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Spare energy sold for $25/MWh</th><td>Near site, by $31k a year</td><td>0 MW wind · 6 MW solar</td><td>5 MW wind · 3 MW solar</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Spare energy sold for $40/MWh</th><td>Windy site, by $93k a year</td><td>0 MW wind · 7 MW solar</td><td>7 MW wind · 8 MW solar</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<!-- cf1-idea:end -->
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><span>The toy's wind and sun take the shapes of SPP's real 2025 hours (<a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">EIA-930</a>), scaled to each site's capacity factor; its costs are illustrative, in 2025 dollars.</span></p>
<p class="lx-datanote"><span>It has no storage and no outages. It assumes the grid takes every spare unit at the chosen price, with no connection limit or extra charge.</span></p>
<div class="lx-xcard">
<header class="lx-x-head"><h3>Two costs pull apart</h3></header>
<table class="cf-two">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Cost</th><th scope="col">What sets it</th><th scope="col">Which site it favours in the toy</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><th scope="row">Site, building and shipping</th><td data-l="What sets it">land prices and the distance to the stores</td><td data-l="Which site it favours">the near site</td></tr>
<tr><th scope="row">Energy, net of sales</th><td data-l="What sets it">the site's wind and sun, the grid's buying price, and what spare energy earns</td><td data-l="Which site it favours">the windy site, once each site can build wind and solar; selling spare energy can make this saving outweigh its higher site and shipping costs</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p class="lx-hint">Every hour counts on its own: energy made when the factory needs none is worth only what the grid pays for it.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">One hour, for example: a 3 MW load with 2 MW made on site buys 1 MW for that hour, which is 1 MWh; with 5 MW made, it sells 2 MWh.</p>
</div>
<div id="cf1-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- cf1-bound:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Where the result holds</p><dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>It holds when</dt><dd><ul><li>stylized supply-chain networks with synthetic distances and costs;</li><li>candidate sites in California, Arizona and Nevada;</li><li>products planned week by week and energy hour by hour over one year;</li><li>the modeled time-of-use tariffs and grid buying and selling prices.</li></ul></dd><dt>It leaves out</dt><dd><ul><li>grid outages, which the studies do not model;</li><li>real distances and costs, which are synthetic.</li></ul></dd></dl><p class="lx-hint">From Li et al. (2023), Applied Mathematical Modelling.</p>
<!-- cf1-bound:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Choosing sites and sizes in one program</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- Opening a site is a yes-or-no choice, so a location model is a [mixed-integer program]{.lx-term term="mixed-integer-program"}: [lesson 10](10-write-it-down.html) introduces decisions, a goal and rules, and [lesson 11](11-solver.html) solves a mixed-integer program.
- The toy above tries every pair of whole-MW sizes at two sites; a solver searches far larger networks without listing every choice.
- Lesson [F7](f07-microgrids.html) builds an hourly energy balance by hand, and Modeler lesson [M5](m05-microgrid-size-and-run.html) sizes a microgrid with a solver.

## Check yourself, then try it
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="cf1-myth">
<!-- cf1-myth:start (written from the toy model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="nearest" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The site nearest the customers is always the cheapest place for a factory.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In the toy, once spare energy earns $40/MWh, the windy site wins by $93k a year, though its site and shipping cost $550k more.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="offgrid" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A factory with its own wind and solar no longer needs the grid.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Even with 7 MW of wind and 8 MW of solar, the windy site still buys 1,881 MWh a year in hours when its wind and solar together fall short of the load, and sells 19,576 MWh.</p></details>
</div>
<!-- cf1-myth:end -->
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-case-try">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Try it yourself</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Optional, about 30 minutes; needs Python on your computer (<a href="b02-python-data.html">lesson B2</a>).</p>
<ul>
<li>Run <code>examples/sensitivity.py</code>. It solves a synthetic supply chain in several cases: compare the benchmark row with "grid supply only". Do the open factories or warehouses change?</li>
<li>Predict first, then read the "purchase price +25%" row: does on-site wind and solar photovoltaic (PV) capacity grow or shrink?</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/supply-chain-microgrid-models">supply-chain-microgrid-models</a>: public example repository · MIT licence · synthetic data.</p>
</div>
```
